intro: A toxicity test, live. Raise the dose and watch what happens to 100 test animals; read the threshold and the LD50 straight off the dose-response curve. Compare three chemicals on one graph (lower LD50, more toxic). Then follow a persistent chemical up a food chain, and keep bioaccumulation (one organism, over time) apart from biomagnification (up the trophic levels).
howItWorks:
The three chemicals are invented for practice. Each curve is a set of measured points (dose in mg per kg of body mass, percent of the test population that died), joined by straight lines; LD50 is read off the curve by the same straight-line reading the exam expects, and the threshold is the highest dose that caused no deaths.

The food chain multiplies the concentration by the same factor at each step up (10 by default), the simple rule exam questions use; real factors vary by chemical and species. The bioaccumulation curve shows one fish taking in a chemical faster than it can excrete it, so its tissue concentration rises with age toward a limit. Concentrations are in parts per million (ppm).

contexts.lead: A lab tests a new garden insecticide.
A company must report how toxic a cleaning solvent is.
A rodent bait is left where a pet dog can reach it.
Seeds treated with a pesticide are spilled near a pond.
A lake was sprayed for mosquitoes with a persistent insecticide years ago.
Mercury from a coal plant settles into a coastal bay.
